chunks: Measuring motor RPM. The question: How can you measure the RPM of a motor?

The usual way to measure a motor's rpm is a sensor that gives pulses as the shaft turns, such as an encoder (a slotted disk read by a light sensor) or a Hall sensor (a magnetic sensor) that sees a magnet go by.
Pulses per second, divided by pulses per revolution, gives revolutions per second, and you multiply by 60 for rpm. The real skill is in how you count the pulses.
You can also get speed from a motor's own back-EMF with no sensor at all.
Think of taking someone's pulse. You can count the beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Or you can time the gap between two beats and divide into 60.
When the heart beats fast, counting for a window works well. When it beats very slowly, you only catch one or two beats in the window, so timing one gap is better.
A pulse train and a gate window.
In the frequency method you count the pulses that fall inside the window (here a handful); with few pulses per window, each missing or extra pulse is a large percentage of the reading.
In the period method you instead count fast clock ticks between two consecutive pulse edges.
PPR: pulses per revolution of the sensor. A single magnet gives 1. Gate (frequency) method: count pulses in a fixed time window. It works well at high speed.
Period method: time the interval between two pulses with a fast clock. It works well at low speed.
Input capture: a timer feature that records the clock value at each pulse edge, so software delays do not add error.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, proportional to speed.
A Hall sensor gives 1 pulse per revolution, and the motor turns at 3000 rpm. That is 50 pulses per second, one every 20 milliseconds.
With a 100 milliseconds window you catch only 5 pulses, and one miscount is a 20% error.
With a 1 megahertz clock timing one pulse period, you count 20,000 ticks, so one tick is only 0. 005%. That is the whole idea.
"I'd get a pulse train from an encoder, a Hall sensor on a magnet, or an optical interrupter, and convert with rpm equals 60 times frequency divided by pulses per rev.
At high speed I count pulses in a fixed window; at low speed I time the period between pulses with a hardware timer. No sensor?
Back-EMF is proportional to speed, so I can measure terminal voltage during a PWM off-time. For lab checks I'd use an optical tach on a reflective mark."
